presenceLabel: Cherokee claim, treaty line or town in this area
presenceNote: 1768 is the Treaty of Hard Labour; 1794 is the Treaty of Tellico Blockhouse. Earlier Cherokee use of Kentucky is real but no dated boundary for it was found, so none is drawn. Chickamauga towns are shown as a county footprint, not a boundary. Kentucky raids are events, not territory, and are not shaded.
overlapNote: The Kentucky area shown here was claimed by several nations at once: Shawnee, Six Nations (Haudenosaunee, by conquest, ceded to the Crown at Fort Stanwix 1768), Chickasaw in the far west, and colonial land companies. Sources disagree on which claim was strongest: Thwaites/Withers call the Cherokee claim "hatched up"; Henderson (1992) says Cherokee used the land with Shawnee permission; the Tennessee Encyclopedia says the Cherokee held the strongest claim; Royce says the extent cannot be defined with accuracy. Treaty lines are cession lines drawn by colonial governments, not maps of who lived where.
basis: Hand-simplified from treaty boundary text (Hard Labor 1768, Lochaber 1770, Donelson 1771, Sycamore Shoals 1775) and Royce (BAE 1887). Native Land Digital data was not used.

eras.label: 1768 · Treaty of Hard Labour
eras.text: On 14 Oct 1768 at Hard Labor, South Carolina, Cherokee leaders and the British Crown agreed a boundary running from the Savannah River to the Reedy River and Tryon Mountain, north to Chiswell’s lead mine, then straight to the mouth of the Kanawha. The treaty text calls it the limits of the lands “reserved by said nation” for their own use. Only the last two legs are drawn (Tryon Mountain to Chiswell’s Mine to Point Pleasant); the line ends in West Virginia, not in Kentucky. The map draws no Cherokee area: sources do not give a dated edge for Cherokee land in Kentucky.

eras.label: 1770 · Treaty of Lochaber
eras.text: On 18 Oct 1770 at Lochaber, South Carolina, the line moved west: along 36°30′ to a point six miles east of Long Island of the Holston, then toward the mouth of the Kanawha. The newly ceded wedge lies almost entirely outside Kentucky (Virginia, Tennessee, North Carolina), so it is shown as a dashed outline only, unfilled. The treaty text has a gap at the last course, so the straight line to Point Pleasant follows the TNGenWeb (Folmsbee) reading. The 1768 line is dashed. Only the part inside Kentucky is the focus here; the rest lies in Virginia, West Virginia and Tennessee, where the edges follow the treaty’s named points and are approximate.

eras.label: 1771 · Donelson survey to the Kentucky River
eras.text: In 1771 surveyor John Donelson ran the line to the head of the Kentucky (“Louisa”) River instead of straight to the Kanawha, then down that river to the Ohio and up the Ohio to the Kanawha. This went beyond the treaty text; TNGenWeb ties it to a promise of £500 that was never paid, and Porterfield v. Clark (U.S. Supreme Court, 1844) quotes a Virginia record saying the line took in more country than the instructions allowed. Hatched = the part of the 1771 survey area that lies inside Kentucky, closed along the Kentucky state boundary (about 29% of the state, eastern Kentucky). This is land the Cherokee gave up (ceded) to Virginia, not a map of where Cherokee people lived. Outside Kentucky only the dashed outline is drawn, at the treaty’s named points (approximate). The Shawnee, who also claimed this ground, were not party to it.

eras.label: 1775 · Sycamore Shoals (private sale)
eras.text: On 17 Mar 1775 Cherokee leaders signed a deed to Richard Henderson’s company (the Transylvania Purchase). The “Great Grant” covered much of Kentucky between the Kentucky and Cumberland rivers. It was a private sale, contrary to the Proclamation of 1763, and it was later annulled: Virginia in 1776 and North Carolina in 1783. The Shawnee did not sign. Two of the deed’s corners are guesses, so the shape is rough. Hatched = the part of the Great Grant inside Kentucky, closed along the Kentucky state boundary; outside Kentucky only a dashed outline. The deed calls are approximate and the sale was later annulled.

eras.label: 1777–1794 · Chickamauga towns
eras.text: Dragging Canoe and followers who rejected the 1777 cession left the older towns in the winter of 1776–77 and settled on Chickamauga Creek near Chattanooga. After militia attacks (1779 in the Tennessee Encyclopedia, 1782 in Wikipedia) they moved farther down the Tennessee to the Five Lower Towns: Running Water, Nickajack, Long Island, Crow Town and Lookout Mountain Town. The shading is a county footprint of the town area, not a boundary. Raids into Kentucky were events and are not shaded. The Treaty of Tellico Blockhouse (8 Nov 1794) ended the fighting.

properties.note: Hard Labour 14 Oct 1768: Savannah/Towatuhe to Reedy River, Tryon Mtn, Chiswell mine, Kanawha mouth. Only Tryon, Chiswell and Point Pleasant are plotted; the Savannah and Reedy legs are omitted. Land west of the line was reserved to the Cherokee.

Lochaber 18 Oct 1770 wedge between the Hard Labour line and the Lochaber line (36.5 N to six miles east of Long Island of the Holston, then straight to the Kanawha mouth). The course between Long Island and the Kanawha is a straight line by assumption; the transcription has a gap ("**").
Lochaber line as drawn: 36.5 N at the Hard Labour line to ~6 mi E of Long Island, then straight to Point Pleasant.

1771 Donelson survey: from the Lochaber line, up the Kentucky ("Louisa") River to its head, down to the Ohio, up the Ohio to the Kanawha. Kentucky River head and North Fork course are hand-simplified. Computed area ~8.2 M acres; Encyclopedia Virginia says ~10 M acres.

Henderson "Great Grant", Sycamore Shoals 17 Mar 1775, read as Ohio (Kentucky mouth to Cumberland mouth), up the Cumberland proper to about Pineville, Powell Mtn ridge (P1 ~36.93N,-82.60 is a guess), then the Kentucky River head and down the Kentucky River. The deed says "including all its waters" for the Cumberland, which would reach further south. Computed ~17 M acres; Tennessee Encyclopedia says 20 M.
Henderson "Path Deed" (NE Tennessee / SW Virginia): Long Island, Big Stone Gap, Cumberland Gap and Powell Mtn are used as corners only as a rough guess; the deed calls were not read in full.
Counties containing the Chickamauga Creek towns and the Five Lower Towns: Hamilton and Marion TN, Dade and Walker GA, Jackson AL. A presence footprint, not a boundary; the counties are modern.
Main-map (Layers toggle) shape: the three sourced treaty/survey lines plus the Chickamauga county footprint. No Cherokee claim frame is drawn for Kentucky.
